questions.q: A $g^r_d$ on a smooth projective curve $C$ is, by definition:
choices: A pair $(L,V)$ with $L$ a line bundle of degree $d$ and $V\subset H^0(C,L)$ an $(r+1)$-dimensional subspace.
A holomorphic differential vanishing to order $d$ at $r$ points.
questions.hint: The $r$ in $g^r_d$ is one less than the dimension of the section space $V$.
questions.explain: A $g^r_d$ is a pair $(L,V)$ with $\deg L=d$ and $\dim V=r+1$. Equivalently it is an $r$-dimensional linear family of effective degree-$d$ divisors on $C$. When $V$ has no base points it defines a morphism $C\to\mathbb{P}(V^*)\cong\mathbb{P}^r$. The distinction matters: a $g^r_d$ is the section-space data, not the morphism (a $g^r_d$ may have base points, in which case it is only rational).

questions.q: A divisor $D$ on $C$ is called special when:
questions.hint: Specialness is about extra sections — beyond what Riemann–Roch forces.
questions.explain: Specialness means $h^1(D) > 0$, equivalently (by Serre duality) $h^0(K-D) > 0$. In the Riemann–Roch formula $h^0(D)-h^1(D)=d-g+1$, a special divisor is one where the correction term $h^1$ is non-zero — i.e. there are extra sections beyond the Riemann–Roch floor. Brill–Noether theory measures how special divisors can be.

questions.q: Select every statement that is correct about the linear series $|D|=\mathbb{P}(H^0(C,\mathcal{O}(D)))$.
choices: $|D|$ parametrises effective divisors linearly equivalent to $D$.
If $|D|$ has no base points, then a choice of basis of $H^0(\mathcal{O}(D))$ defines a morphism $C\to\mathbb{P}^r$.
questions.hint: Two of the five are simply false — $|D|$ can be empty (when $h^0=0$), and its size depends on $g$ even for large $d$.
questions.explain: The first three are core definitions: $|D|$ is the projectivisation of the section space, has projective dimension $h^0-1$, and (when basepoint-free) defines a morphism. The fourth is false: $|D|=\emptyset$ whenever $h^0(\mathcal{O}(D))=0$ — for example any negative-degree $D$. The fifth is false: for $d>2g-2$ we have $h^0(D)=d-g+1$, which depends on both $d$ and $g$.

questions.q: On a smooth projective curve of genus $g=5$, what is $h^0(\mathcal{O}(D))$ for a generic divisor $D$ of degree $d=10$?
questions.hint: $d>2g-2$, so Serre vanishing makes $D$ non-special.
questions.explain: We have $d=10$ and $2g-2=8$, so $d>2g-2$ and Serre vanishing gives $h^1(D)=h^0(K-D)=0$. Riemann–Roch then forces $h^0(D)=d-g+1=10-5+1=6$ exactly. In the non-special range, Riemann–Roch is an equality, not just a lower bound.

questions.q: For a smooth projective curve of genus $g$ and the canonical divisor $K$, $h^0(K)$ equals:
questions.hint: $\Omega^1_C$ is the canonical bundle and $H^0(C,\Omega^1_C)$ has dimension $g$ by definition.
questions.explain: By definition of the genus, $H^0(C,\Omega^1_C) = H^0(C,K)$ has dimension $g$. Riemann–Roch with $D=K$ reads $h^0(K)-h^0(0)=(2g-2)-g+1=g-1$, so $h^0(K)=g+h^0(0)-1$. With $h^0(\mathcal{O}_C)=1$ this gives $h^0(K)=g$, consistent. The canonical divisor is the universal example of a special divisor with maximal $h^1$.

questions.q: Consider the following Riemann–Roch computation for $D$ a degree-$3$ divisor on a smooth curve of genus $g=4$: 'Since $d=3<2g-2=6$, $D$ is special. By Riemann–Roch, $h^0(D)=d-g+1=0$. So $|D|$ is empty.' Where does the argument go wrong?
choices: $d=3$ is not in the special range for $g=4$.

Riemann–Roch gives $h^0(D)-h^1(D)=d-g+1=0$, but the conclusion $h^0=0$ ignores $h^1\ge 0$. In the special range, $h^1(D)>0$ is possible, and $h^0=h^1$ above the Riemann–Roch floor — RR is a lower bound on $h^0$, not an equality, when $D$ is special.
$h^0$ is always at least $1$ for any divisor.
The canonical divisor has degree $2g$, not $2g-2$.
questions.hint: Riemann–Roch is $h^0-h^1=d-g+1$, not $h^0=d-g+1$.
questions.explain: In the special range, $h^1(D)>0$ is exactly the phenomenon that lets $h^0$ exceed the Riemann–Roch floor. For a degree-$3$ divisor on a genus-$4$ curve, the trigonal pencil example has $h^0(D)=2$ (a $g^1_3$) and $h^1(D)=2$, so $h^0-h^1=0=d-g+1$ — but $h^0$ is $2$, not $0$. Riemann–Roch alone bounds $h^0\ge \max(0,d-g+1)$; you need to actually compute $h^1$ (or invoke Brill–Noether) to know $h^0$.

questions.q: Compute $\rho(g,r,d)$ for $(g,r,d)=(7,1,4)$.
questions.explain: $g - d + r = 7 - 4 + 1 = 4$, so $(r+1)(g-d+r) = 2\cdot 4 = 8$, and $\rho = 7 - 8 = -1$. Since $\rho<0$, a general genus-$7$ curve has no $g^1_4$ (degree-4 map to $\mathbb{P}^1$). The locus $\mathcal{M}^1_{7,4}\subset\mathcal{M}_7$ of tetragonal curves of genus $7$ is then a Brill–Noether divisor — codimension exactly $|\rho|=1$ in $\mathcal{M}_7$.

questions.q: On a general smooth projective curve of genus $g$, the Brill–Noether number $\rho(g,r,d)$ tells you:
choices: The expected dimension of the variety of $g^r_d$'s; positive $\rho$ predicts existence, negative $\rho$ predicts emptiness.
The genus of the image curve in $\mathbb{P}^r$.
The degree of the canonical embedding.
questions.hint: $\rho$ is the dimension of $W^r_d$, not its cardinality.
questions.explain: $\rho(g,r,d)$ is the expected (and on a general curve, actual) dimension of $W^r_d(C)$. When $\rho<0$ this means $W^r_d(C)=\emptyset$ on a general curve; when $\rho\ge 0$, the Brill–Noether theorem (Kempf, Kleiman–Laksov) says it is non-empty. The actual count of $g^r_d$'s (when $\rho=0$) is given by a Castelnuovo number — a specific Schubert intersection — but $\rho$ itself is the dimension.

questions.q: Match each $(g,r,d)$ triple to the geometric reading of $\rho(g,r,d)$ on a general curve.
right: $\rho=0$: unique $g^1_2$; every genus-2 curve is hyperelliptic.
$\rho=1$: every curve has a 1-parameter family of $g^1_4$'s.
$\rho=0$: a $g^1_3$ exists (trigonal pencil), with finitely many on a general curve.
$\rho=-1$: a general genus-3 curve has no $g^1_2$ — the hyperelliptic locus is a divisor in $\mathcal{M}_3$.
questions.explain: $\rho(2,1,2)=2-2\cdot 1=0$ (unique $g^1_2$; every genus-2 curve is hyperelliptic). $\rho(3,1,2)=3-2\cdot 2=-1$ (the hyperelliptic locus is a divisor in $\mathcal{M}_3$). $\rho(4,1,3)=4-2\cdot 2=0$ (every genus-4 curve has a $g^1_3$, with a 2-element family on a general curve, by Castelnuovo). $\rho(5,1,4)=5-2\cdot 2=1$ (every curve has a 1-parameter family of $g^1_4$'s).

questions.q: $W^r_d(C)$ is defined as a subset of which ambient variety?
questions.hint: $W^r_d$ is a locus inside the space of degree-$d$ line bundles on $C$.
questions.explain: $W^r_d(C)\subseteq\Pic^d(C)$ is the set of line bundles $L$ of degree $d$ on $C$ with $h^0(L)\ge r+1$. The Picard variety has dimension $g$, and $W^r_d$ cuts out a subvariety of expected codimension $(r+1)(g-d+r)$. The closely related space $G^r_d(C)$ — pairs $(L,V)$ rather than just $L$ — sits over $W^r_d$ and parametrises the actual $g^r_d$'s; the projection $G^r_d\to W^r_d$ is birational outside $W^{r+1}_d$.

questions.q: The expected codimension of $W^r_d(C)$ in $\Pic^d(C)$ is $(r+1)(g-d+r)$. For $(g,r,d)=(8,2,7)$, what is this codimension?
questions.explain: $(r+1)(g-d+r)=(2+1)(8-7+2)=3\cdot 3=9$. So the expected codimension is $9$, but $\dim\Pic^d=g=8$ — the codimension exceeds the dimension, so $W^2_7(C)=\emptyset$ on a general genus-$8$ curve. Consistently, $\rho(8,2,7)=8-9=-1$.

questions.q: $W^r_d(C)$ has a natural scheme structure because it is:
choices: A homogeneous space under a Lie group action.
A determinantal subscheme — cut out by a rank condition on a map of vector bundles $\gamma\colon\mathcal{F}\to\mathcal{G}$ on $\Pic^d(C)$.
A complete intersection of explicit polynomials.
questions.hint: $h^0(L)\ge r+1$ is a rank-drop condition on an evaluation-of-sections map.
questions.explain: Choose a Poincaré bundle on $C\times\Pic^d(C)$ and a sufficiently positive effective divisor $E$ on $C$. Pushforward along the second projection gives a map of vector bundles $\gamma\colon\mathcal{F}\to\mathcal{G}$ on $\Pic^d(C)$, and the fibre rank-drop of $\gamma$ at $L$ measures $h^0(L)$. The locus where $\operatorname{rk}\gamma\le\operatorname{rk}\mathcal{F}-(r+1)$ — i.e. $h^0(L)\ge r+1$ — is then a determinantal subscheme, cut by $(r+1)\times(r+1)$ minors. This is how Macaulay/Porteous gives the expected codimension.

questions.q: The Brill–Noether existence theorem (Kempf 1971 / Kleiman–Laksov 1972) asserts that $W^r_d(C)$ is non-empty:
choices: For every smooth projective curve $C$, whenever $\rho(g,r,d)\ge 0$.
questions.hint: Existence is unconditional — it holds for any curve once $\rho\ge 0$.
questions.explain: The non-emptiness half of Brill–Noether is unconditional: every smooth projective curve of genus $g$ carries a $g^r_d$ whenever $\rho(g,r,d)\ge 0$. The proof is a Schubert / Chern-class computation: the class of $W^r_d$ in $H^*(\Pic^d)$ is a positive Schur polynomial, hence non-zero. The 'general curve' refinement is for the dimension: $\dim W^r_d=\rho$ on a general curve, but on a special curve the dimension can jump.

questions.q: Arrange the steps of the Kempf / Kleiman–Laksov existence proof in the standard order.
items: Push $\mathcal{P}$ (twisted) forward along $\pi_2$ to get a map $\gamma\colon\mathcal{F}\to\mathcal{G}$ on $\Pic^d(C)$.
Identify $W^r_d$ as the determinantal locus where $\operatorname{rk}\gamma$ drops by $\ge r+1$.
Apply Macaulay/Porteous to express $[W^r_d]\in H^*(\Pic^d)$ as a Schur polynomial in Chern classes.
Verify the Schur polynomial is non-zero (positive coefficients) whenever $\rho\ge 0$, hence $W^r_d\ne\emptyset$.
questions.hint: Build the universal object, push forward, identify the locus, compute the class, then evaluate.
questions.explain: The five steps form the proof in order: (1) Build a universal degree-$d$ line bundle parametrised over $\Pic^d$. (2) Pushforward gives a comparison map of bundles whose fibre rank is $h^0$. (3) The determinantal locus is set-theoretically $W^r_d$. (4) Macaulay/Porteous gives an explicit class — a Schur polynomial — in cohomology. (5) Positivity of the Schur polynomial coefficients (when $\rho\ge 0$) forces the class to be non-zero, which forces the locus to be non-empty. The argument is Chern-class machinery applied universally; the geometric input is just 'a Poincaré bundle exists'.

questions.q: On a general smooth projective curve $C$ of genus $g$, what is $\dim W^r_d(C)$ when $\rho(g,r,d)\ge 0$?
questions.hint: On a general curve, the expected dimension is the actual dimension.
questions.explain: Griffiths–Harris (1980) sharpened existence: on a general curve, $\dim W^r_d(C)=\rho(g,r,d)$ exactly when $\rho\ge 0$. The 'expected' dimension matches the actual one. On special curves, $\dim W^r_d$ can exceed $\rho$ — those are the curves living in proper subvarieties of $\mathcal{M}_g$, and they include the classical loci (hyperelliptic, trigonal, etc.).

questions.q: The Petri map $\mu_0(L)$ at $L\in W^r_d(C)$ is:
choices: The evaluation map $H^0(L)\to L_p$ at a point $p$.
The dual of the Abel–Jacobi map.
The restriction of a line bundle to a subcurve.
questions.hint: Multiply a section of $L$ by a section of $K\otimes L^{-1}$ to get a section of $K$.
questions.explain: The Petri map $\mu_0(L)\colon H^0(C,L)\otimes H^0(C,K\otimes L^{-1})\to H^0(C,K)$ is the cup-product (multiplication of sections, valued in the canonical bundle since $L\otimes(K\otimes L^{-1})=K$). Its cokernel is the Zariski cotangent space to $W^r_d$ at $L$, and Petri's theorem asserts $\mu_0$ is injective on a general curve.

questions.q: Petri's theorem (Gieseker 1982) says: on a general smooth projective curve $C$, for $L$ in the open stratum $W^r_d\setminus W^{r+1}_d$, the Petri map $\mu_0(L)$ is injective. The consequence is:
choices: $W^r_d(C)$ is smooth at $L$ of dimension exactly $\rho(g,r,d)$.
questions.hint: The cokernel of $\mu_0$ is the cotangent space to $W^r_d$; injectivity makes cotangent dimension minimal.
questions.explain: The Zariski cotangent space $T^*_L W^r_d=\operatorname{coker}\mu_0(L)^*$, so $\dim T_L W^r_d=\dim\operatorname{coker}\mu_0$. When $\mu_0$ is injective (rank = $\dim\operatorname{domain}=(r+1)(g-d+r)$), $\dim\operatorname{coker}=g-(r+1)(g-d+r)=\rho$. So $W^r_d$ is smooth of dimension exactly $\rho$ at $L$. Petri (proved by Gieseker, then more cleanly by Eisenbud–Harris via limit linear series) says this happens generically.

questions.q: On a general smooth projective curve of genus $g=8$, what is the dimension of $W^2_7$? (Compute $\rho$.)
questions.explain: $\rho(8,2,7) = 8 - 3\cdot(8-7+2) = 8 - 3\cdot 3 = -1$. Since $\rho<0$, $W^2_7(C)$ is empty on a general curve. The locus $\{C\in\mathcal{M}_8:W^2_7(C)\ne\emptyset\}$ — curves of genus 8 with a $g^2_7$ (a plane septic) — is a Brill–Noether divisor, of codimension $|\rho|=1$ in $\mathcal{M}_8$.

questions.q: When $\rho(g,r,d)=-1$, the locus $\mathcal{M}^r_{g,d}=\{[C]\in\mathcal{M}_g:W^r_d(C)\ne\emptyset\}$ is:
choices: A divisor (codim 1) in $\mathcal{M}_g$ — the Brill–Noether divisor.
questions.hint: $|\rho|$ is the codimension of the failure locus in $\mathcal{M}_g$.
questions.explain: For $\rho=-1$, the locus of curves where $W^r_d$ is non-empty (against the generic expectation) has codimension $1$ in $\mathcal{M}_g$ — it is a divisor. These are the Brill–Noether divisors; Eisenbud–Harris (1987) computed their classes in $\Pic(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_g)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ as explicit combinations of $\lambda$ and the boundary classes $\delta_i$, using limit linear series on flag curves. For more negative $\rho$, the locus has higher codimension.

questions.q: The Eisenbud–Harris theory of limit linear series extends Brill–Noether to:
choices: Smooth curves over fields of positive characteristic.
Stable nodal curves at the boundary of $\overline{\mathcal{M}}_g$ — letting one compute Brill–Noether divisor classes by degeneration.
questions.hint: Eisenbud–Harris's technical innovation was handling the boundary $\partial\overline{\mathcal{M}}_g$.
questions.explain: A limit linear series on a chain of components prescribes a coordinated choice of linear series on each component, with vanishing-sequence compatibility at the nodes. Eisenbud–Harris (1986) showed limit linear series on flag curves (chains of elliptic curves) smooth out to $g^r_d$'s on nearby smooth curves — proving Petri by degeneration and supplying explicit divisor classes in $\Pic\overline{\mathcal{M}}_g\otimes\mathbb{Q}$. The classes are the central technical input to the Harris–Mumford theorem on the Kodaira dimension of $\overline{\mathcal{M}}_g$.

questions.q: Select every $(g,r,d)$ triple with $\rho(g,r,d)=-1$ — i.e. giving a Brill–Noether divisor in $\mathcal{M}_g$.
choices: $(4,1,3)$ — trigonal pencils on a genus-4 curve.
questions.hint: Compute $\rho$ for each; the $\rho=-1$ cases are exactly the codim-$1$ loci in $\mathcal{M}_g$.
questions.explain: $\rho(3,1,2)=3-2\cdot 2=-1$ ✓ (hyperelliptic divisor in $\mathcal{M}_3$). $\rho(4,1,3)=4-2\cdot 2=0$ (every genus-4 curve has a $g^1_3$, so the locus is all of $\mathcal{M}_4$ — not a divisor). $\rho(5,1,3)=5-2\cdot 3=-1$ ✓ (trigonal divisor in $\mathcal{M}_5$). $\rho(7,1,4)=7-2\cdot 4=-1$ ✓ (tetragonal divisor in $\mathcal{M}_7$). $\rho(2,1,2)=0$ (unique $g^1_2$ on every genus-2 curve — not a divisor). The pattern: $\rho(2k+1,1,k+1)=-1$ gives the classic codimension-1 'gonality' loci in odd genus, with classes computed explicitly by Harris–Mumford and Eisenbud–Harris.
